title: Take Home Ex2: VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 2
text:
In this exercise, Mini-Challenge 2 of VAST Challenge 2026 is tackled.
The following questions are addressed:

Q1. How was the anomalous SaidIT post made? A visual tool is built to describe the sequence of events leading up to the post, including people and system interactions.

Q1a. A detailed view of the exact chain of events for this message of interest is provided.
Q1b. A system overview that contextualises this message chain in the overall system is provided.



Q2. What do the posts “mean”? The origin of the post contents is investigated, with reasoning illustrated behind the assertion of their meaning and probable content.


Q3. Could this behaviour repeat?

Q3a. Historic system behaviour is investigated to find other instances, with prior occurrences illustrated and contrasted with the most recent one.
Q3b. Possible system changes that would make recurrence more difficult are illustrated, with at most one intervention point identified and justified using visual analytics.










WarningIncident Report — SaidIT Anomalous Publication



On 17 May 2046 at 11:21 UTC, a post appeared on SaidIT published under the identity of John Windward, Head of Customer Support at Tenant Thread. The post was written in gibberish and appeared in an apparently random forum — raising immediate concern that an AI agent had malfunctioned or been manipulated.


This report investigates the incident systematically. The analysis progresses from understanding the full system, to establishing a normal baseline, to isolating the anomaly, tracing its exact chain, and finally recommending one targeted remedy.

TipHow to Navigate This Report



The analysis follows the incident from start to finish — system mapping first, then the anomaly, then prevention. Code is hidden by default; click “Show code” on any section to see the full implementation. Coloured callout boxes highlight key observations (blue), methodology notes (green), limitations (red), and important findings (orange).





The investigation proceeds in eight sequential steps, each building on the previous one. Rather than jumping to conclusions, the analysis first establishes what is normal before identifying what is not.
Step 1 — Map overall system activity All action types, actors, and timing patterns are characterised across the full event log. This ensures the investigation is grounded in the complete picture before any filtering is applied.
Step 2 — Establish a behavioural baseline A determination is made of what normal SaidIT posting looks like — who posts, how often, what the content structure contains, and what events precede and follow a normal post.
Step 3 — Identify the anomalous post The baseline is used to formally show why John Windward’s 17 May post deviates from normal behaviour. The deviation must be demonstrable, not assumed.
Step 4 — Trace the exact event chain The sequence of events is traced backwards from the post — through agents, files, and task delegations — to identify every step that contributed to the anomalous publication.
Step 5 — Contextualise within the wider system The identified chain is positioned within the full organisational and agent network to show whether the route was unusual or followed common system pathways.
Step 6 — Investigate content provenance Observable evidence from the event log — file sizes, creation timing, routing and deletion patterns — is used to make defensible inferences about the probable origin of the post content.
Step 7 — Search for historical recurrence The detection signature established in Step 2 is applied to the entire event history to determine whether similar incidents occurred before 17 May.
Step 8 — Design one intervention The single most effective control point is identified, verified using historical data that all suspicious posts pass through it, and the outcome of applying the control is simulated.



The eight steps above are summarised in the roadmap below, grouped into four analytical phases.

text:
3.1 Extracting and Tidying the Event Table
Relevant fields are extracted from the raw JSON structure and create derived variables covering time, attack identity, actor type, and action category.


Show the full event tidying pipeline
ev_raw    <- raw_data$events
detail_df <- ev_raw$details

events <- tibble(
  event_id      = ev_raw$id,
  short_name    = ev_raw$short_name,
  when          = ev_raw$when,
  parties       = ev_raw$parties,
  d_poster_id   = detail_df$poster_id,
  d_person      = detail_df$person,
  d_content     = detail_df$content,
  d_content_src = detail_df$content_source,
  d_target_agt  = detail_df$target_agent,
  d_args_path   = detail_df$args$path,
  d_target      = detail_df$target,
  d_action      = detail_df$action,
  d_forum       = detail_df$forum,
  d_task        = detail_df$task,
  d_from        = detail_df$from,
  d_to          = detail_df$to
) %>%
  mutate(
    event_time  = as_datetime(when),
    event_date  = as_date(event_time),
    event_hour  = hour(event_time),
    event_wday  = wday(event_time, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
    attack_tag  = case_when(
      (!is.na(d_args_path) & str_detect(d_args_path, "HiddenOrca"))  |
      (!is.na(d_target)    & str_detect(d_target,    "HiddenOrca"))   ~ "HiddenOrca",
      (!is.na(d_args_path) & str_detect(d_args_path, "MellowOtter")) |
      (!is.na(d_target)    & str_detect(d_target,    "MellowOtter"))  ~ "MellowOtter",
      (!is.na(d_args_path) & str_detect(d_args_path, "SwiftWren"))   |
      (!is.na(d_target)    & str_detect(d_target,    "SwiftWren"))    ~ "SwiftWren",
      !is.na(d_content_src) ~ str_remove(d_content_src, "\\.txt$"),
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    is_anomalous = !is.na(d_content_src),
    is_moi       = is_anomalous & str_detect(coalesce(d_content_src,""), "SwiftWren"),
    actor_type   = case_when(
      map_lgl(parties, ~ any(str_detect(.x, "^Agent/person:"))) ~ "Agent",
      map_lgl(parties, ~ any(str_detect(.x, "^person:")))       ~ "Person",
      TRUE                                                        ~ "System"
    ),
    action_cat = case_when(
      short_name %in% c("read_file","access_files","list_files","check_access") ~ "Document Access",
      short_name == "create_file"                                                ~ "File Creation",
      short_name == "delete_file"                                                ~ "File Deletion",
      short_name %in% c("queue_subordinate_task","assign_agent_task",
                        "give_advice","ask_agent")                               ~ "Agent Communication",
      short_name %in% c("post_saidit","saidit_post","post_flex",
                        "flex_post","saidit_post_check")                         ~ "External Publication",
      short_name %in% c("sent","received","check_email",
                        "access_email","send_email")                             ~ "Email / Comms",
      TRUE                                                                        ~ "Meetings / Presence"
    )
  )

# Helper functions
get_agent  <- function(v) { h <- grep("^Agent/person:", v, value=TRUE); if(length(h)) gsub("Agent/person:","",h[1]) else NA_character_ }
get_person <- function(v) { h <- grep("^person:",       v, value=TRUE); if(length(h)) gsub("person:",      "",h[1]) else NA_character_ }

text:
8.3 Betweenness Centrality — Key Relay Agents






TipWhy Betweenness Centrality?



Betweenness centrality identifies agents who lie on the shortest path between others, but it does not capture all forms of influence in the propagation network. For example, an agent who forwarded the instruction many times to the same target would have high transmission frequency but low betweenness.
Other measures that could complement this analysis include degree centrality (total number of hops sent) and eigenvector centrality (influence weighted by the influence of neighbours). However, for the purposes of this investigation, betweenness centrality is sufficient to identify the key relay agents — those whose removal or monitoring would have the greatest impact on containment.




Show the code for betweenness centrality analysis
swift_ig <- graph_from_data_frame(swift_edges, directed = TRUE)
betw     <- betweenness(swift_ig, directed = TRUE, normalized = TRUE)
deg_in   <- degree(swift_ig, mode = "in")
deg_out  <- degree(swift_ig, mode = "out")

cent_df <- tibble(
  agent       = names(betw),
  betweenness = betw,
  degree_in   = deg_in[names(betw)],
  degree_out  = deg_out[names(betw)],
  role        = case_when(
    agent == "john_windward" ~ "Target",
    agent == "emma_harbor"   ~ "Origin",
    TRUE ~ "Propagator")
) %>% arrange(desc(betweenness))

cent_df %>%
  mutate(agent = fct_reorder(agent, betweenness)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(betweenness, agent, fill = role)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(betweenness, 3)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Target="#f4a261", Origin=STYLES$success,
                                Propagator=STYLES$primary)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title   = "Betweenness Centrality — SwiftWren Worm Network",
       subtitle = "Higher betweenness = more critical relay point in the propagation chain",
       x = "Normalised betweenness centrality", y = NULL, fill = "Role",
       caption  = "Source: MC2 data.json") +
  THEME_MC2 + theme(legend.position = "top")











Show the code for the interactive centrality table
cent_df %>%
  select(Agent=agent, Role=role, Betweenness=betweenness,
         `Degree In`=degree_in, `Degree Out`=degree_out) %>%
  mutate(Betweenness = round(Betweenness, 4)) %>%
  DT::datatable(
    caption  = "Agent centrality measures — click column headers to sort",
    options  = list(pageLength=10, scrollX=TRUE),
    rownames = FALSE, filter = "top"
  ) %>%
  DT::formatStyle("Role",
    backgroundColor = DT::styleEqual(
      c("Target","Origin","Propagator"),
      c("#ffe0b2","#c8e6c9","#e3f2fd")))












NoteObservations




zoey_drydock (0.146) and evelyn_dock (0.14) have the highest betweenness, they were the most critical relay points in the propagation chain, sitting on the shortest paths between the most agents.
chloe_ballast (0.116) ranks third and is notable as the agent who delivered the final instruction directly to john_windward.
emma_harbor (Origin) has zero betweenness, she started the chain but immediately passed it on, playing no further relay role.
john_windward (Target) also has near-zero betweenness (0.0025), he received the instruction but never forwarded it, consistent with his role as the final executor.
gabriel_sonar has the highest degree in (10) despite moderate betweenness meaning many agents sent instructions to him, but he was not always on the shortest path between them.









NoteLimitations of Betweenness Centrality



Betweenness centrality identifies agents on the shortest path between others, but does not capture all forms of influence. An agent like gabriel_sonar who received instructions from 10 different agents would not score highly on betweenness but was clearly heavily involved in the propagation. Other measures such as degree centrality or eigenvector centrality could complement this analysis, but for the purposes of identifying key relay points, betweenness centrality is sufficient.

11.1 The Recommended Intervention Point






WarningOne Intervention Only



Only one change is recommended. Rather than redesigning the entire system, the fix targets a single existing step — the moment just before a post goes live on SaidIT. This step already exists in the system, so no new infrastructure is needed.


The intervention does not require redesigning the agent network and it stops harm at the last possible moment without disrupting internal operation. The saidit_post_check event already fires before every SaidIT post. We simply upgrade it to evaluate three additional observable signals:
EXISTING CHECK:
saidit_post_check → Does this agent have SaidIT permission? → YES → post proceeds

UPGRADED CHECK:
saidit_post_check → Does this agent have SaidIT permission? → YES
                  → Is content coming from content_source (a file)? → YES ⛔
                  → Was there a peer-agent task chain just before? → YES ⛔
                  → Is a delete_file action queued immediately after? → YES ⛔
                  → ALL 3 signals present → HOLD for human review

5.1 Target Variables
The target variables are loss_ratio, claim_frequency, total_incurred and has_claim, which measure portfolio profitability, volatility, claim severity and claim occurrence respectively. As some variables contain extreme outliers, the analysis is restricted to a reasonable range for visualisation purposes. Before diving into the Exploratory Data Analysis, the distributions of key variables are examined individually to better understand their characteristics and identify any notable patterns.

Loss RatioClaim Frequency


loss_ratio measures the ratio of total incurred costs to total premium collected. A loss ratio greater than 1 indicates that the insurer paid out more in claims than it collected in premiums.
A raincloud plot is used here as it combines a half-violin density plot, boxplot and individual data points into a single view, providing a more complete picture of the distribution than a histogram or boxplot alone — simultaneously showing shape, central tendency, spread and outliers.

insurance_lr <- insurance %>%
  filter(loss_ratio < 10,
         loss_ratio > 0)

ggplot(insurance_lr,
       aes(x = 0, y = loss_ratio)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA,
               fill = "#4a7c6f") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2,
               outlier.shape = NA,
               fill = "#7aadab",
               alpha = 0.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Loss Ratio",
       subtitle = "Policies with loss ratio between 0 and 10",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Loss Ratio") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank())








The raincloud plot reveals that loss_ratio is highly right-skewed among policies with claims. Most policies record a loss ratio between 1.0 and 2.5, indicating that incurred costs typically exceed premiums collected. The long right tail suggests that a small number of policies experience exceptionally high losses, which significantly impacts overall portfolio profitability.
A histogram paired with a boxplot is used below to complement the raincloud plot — the histogram reveals the precise frequency distribution while the boxplot highlights the median and interquartile range in a compact format.

             aes(x = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1,
                 fill = "#4a7c6f",
                 colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(loss_ratio)),
             colour = "red",
             linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(loss_ratio)),
             colour = "blue",
             linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(insurance_lr$loss_ratio) + 0.3,
           y = Inf, vjust = 2,
           label = paste("Mean:", round(mean(insurance_lr$loss_ratio), 2)),
           colour = "red", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = median(insurance_lr$loss_ratio) + 0.3,
           y = Inf, vjust = 4,
           label = paste("Median:", round(median(insurance_lr$loss_ratio), 2)),
           colour = "blue", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Loss Ratio",
       x = "Loss Ratio",
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

             aes(x = loss_ratio,
                 y = "")) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#7aadab",
               outlier.alpha = 0.3,

  labs(x = "Loss Ratio",

The distribution of loss_ratio is highly right-skewed, with the majority of policies having a loss ratio of 0 (no claims made). The mean loss ratio is higher than the median, indicating the presence of a small number of policies with very high loss ratios that pull the mean upward.

ECDF of Incurred Amount by Policy Type
An Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function (ECDF) plot is used below to complement the histogram. Unlike a histogram where the shape can change depending on bin width, the ECDF makes no such assumption, it shows directly what proportion of claims fall below any given cost level for each policy type, making it easier to compare tail behaviour across groups at a glance.

insurance %>%
  filter(total_incurred > 0, total_incurred < 10000) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total_incurred, colour = policy_type)) +
  stat_ecdf(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Comprehensive with Excess"    = "#4a7c6f",
    "Comprehensive without Excess" = "#7aadab",
    "Third-Party"                  = "#d4e8e1",
    "Third-Party Combined"         = "#2d5a51",
    "Third-Party with Glass"       = "#a8d5c2")) +
  labs(title = "ECDF of Total Incurred by Policy Type",
       subtitle = "Policies with total incurred between €0 and €10,000",
       x = "Total Incurred (€)",
       y = "Cumulative Proportion",
       colour = "Policy Type") +
  theme_minimal()








The ECDF plot shows that all five policy types follow a broadly similar distribution, with most claims concentrated below €2,500. Third-Party with Glass and Comprehensive without Excess curves rise more steeply in the lower cost range, indicating a higher proportion of small, cheap claims, consistent with the finding that the absence of an excess encourages filing of minor claims. Comprehensive with Excess and Third-Party Combined have slightly flatter curves, suggesting a wider spread of claim costs including a larger proportion of mid-to-high cost claims. Third-Party shows the most gradual curve, indicating the greatest spread of claim costs across the full range though its small sample size means this should be interpreted with caution.

If this trend continues, the portfolio could approach or breach the break-even point in future years, making it important to investigate and address the underlying loss drivers now.

text:
6.3 Factors Affecting Loss Ratio (Profitability)
loss_ratio is used as the measure of portfolio profitability. Only policies with a loss ratio between 0 and 10 are included to exclude extreme outliers that may distort the analysis.
ggbetweenstats() of the ggstatsplot package is used throughout this section as it integrates the visual comparison of group distributions with the results of a nonparametric statistical test in a single figure. The nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis test is chosen because loss_ratio is non-normally distributed and right-skewed, violating the normality assumption required for ANOVA.

Bonus ScorePolicy TypeFuel TypeCirculation AreaDriver Age


The violin plot below examines whether bonus_score — reflecting a policyholder’s past claims history — has a significant effect on loss_ratio.

ggbetweenstats(
  data = insurance_lr,
  x    = bonus_score,
  y    = loss_ratio,
  type = "nonparametric",
  mean.ci = TRUE,
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "significant",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  messages = FALSE,
  title = "Loss Ratio by Bonus Score",
  xlab = "Bonus Score",
  ylab = "Loss Ratio",
  palette = "Set2"
)








The Kruskal-Wallis test confirms a statistically significant difference in loss ratio across bonus score groups (p = 2.07e-19). Interestingly, policyholders with a Good bonus score have the highest median loss ratio of 2.02, followed by Neutral (1.60) and Bad (1.44). This counterintuitive finding may be attributed to the fact that Good bonus score policyholders dominate the portfolio (n = 35,663) and tend to hold more comprehensive policies, which attract higher claim costs. All pairwise comparisons are statistically significant, confirming that bonus score is a meaningful differentiator of portfolio profitability.


The violin plot below examines whether policy_type has a significant effect on loss_ratio.

ggbetweenstats(
  data = insurance_lr,
  x    = policy_type,
  y    = loss_ratio,
  type = "nonparametric",
  mean.ci = TRUE,
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "significant",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  messages = FALSE,
  title = "Loss Ratio by Policy Type",
  xlab = "Policy Type",
  ylab = "Loss Ratio",
  palette = "Set2"
)








The Kruskal-Wallis test confirms a statistically significant difference in loss ratio across policy types (p = 5.09e-92). The Third-Party policy type has the highest median loss ratio of 4.29 (n = 241), which is notably higher than all other policy types. Among the remaining policy types, Third-Party Combined (2.25) and Third-Party with Glass (2.22) have higher median loss ratios compared to Comprehensive with Excess (1.74) and Comprehensive without Excess (1.78).



ggbetweenstats(
  data = insurance_lr,
  x    = fuel_type,
  y    = loss_ratio,

text:
6.5 Distribution Comparison across Key Groups
To complement the statistical analysis in Sections 6.3 and 6.4, ridgeline plots are used to compare the full distribution of loss_ratio and claim_frequency across key grouping variables. Ridgeline plots are chosen here as they allow simultaneous comparison of full distribution shapes across multiple groups — revealing modality, skewness and tail behaviour that boxplots alone cannot convey.

Loss Ratio by Policy TypeClaim Frequency by Bonus Score



insurance_lr %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio,
             y = policy_type,
             fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.7,
                      scale = 0.9,
                      quantile_lines = TRUE,
                      quantiles = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Comprehensive with Excess"    = "#4a7c6f",
    "Comprehensive without Excess" = "#7aadab",
    "Third-Party"                  = "#d4e8e1",
    "Third-Party Combined"         = "#2d5a51",
    "Third-Party with Glass"       = "#a8d5c2")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Loss Ratio by Policy Type",
       subtitle = "Vertical line shows median",
       x = "Loss Ratio",
       y = "Policy Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








The ridgeline plot provides a clearer view of how loss ratio distributions differ across policy types. Comprehensive with Excess and Third-Party Combined show the narrowest and most concentrated distributions, peaking sharply around 1–2, indicating consistent and predictable loss behaviour. Most notably, Third-Party policies exhibit a distinctive bimodal distribution with two peaks, one around 1–2 and another around 4–5, suggesting two distinct subgroups with very different loss behaviours.



insurance_cf %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = claim_frequency,
             y = bonus_score,
             fill = bonus_score)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.7,
                      scale = 0.9,
                      quantile_lines = TRUE,
                      quantiles = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Good"    = "#4a7c6f",
    "Neutral" = "#7aadab",
    "Bad"     = "#d4e8e1")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Claim Frequency by Bonus Score",
       subtitle = "Vertical line shows median",
       x = "Claim Frequency",
       y = "Bonus Score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








The ridgeline plot clearly shows distinct distribution shapes across bonus score groups. Good bonus score policies show a sharp, concentrated peak around 1. Bad bonus score policies show the widest and most right-skewed distribution, with a long tail extending beyond 6, visually confirming the statistical findings from Section 6.4 that policyholders with a poor claims history exhibit the most unpredictable claim behaviour in the portfolio.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Uncovering Loss Drivers in Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio using Data Visualisation
text:
Key Findings
Portfolio Overview
The portfolio is dominated by middle-aged drivers holding Third-Party Combined policies, with the vast majority of policyholders recording no claims. This suggests a generally low-risk customer base, with a small but significant minority of high-risk policyholders driving most of the portfolio’s losses.
Profitability (Loss Ratio)
Policy type emerges as the strongest differentiator of portfolio profitability. Basic Third-Party policies are the least profitable despite being the least common, while Comprehensive with Excess policies generate the most consistent and stable loss ratios. This suggests that broader coverage does not necessarily translate to higher losses — comprehensive policyholders tend to be more careful drivers who pay higher premiums.
Fuel type and circulation area, while statistically significant, have negligible practical impact on profitability and are unlikely to be meaningful underwriting factors on their own.
Volatility (Claim Frequency)
Bonus score is the most powerful predictor of claim frequency. Policyholders with a Bad bonus score make significantly more frequent claims, contributing disproportionately to portfolio volatility. This confirms that past claims history is a reliable indicator of future claim behaviour.
Comprehensive without Excess policies stand out as the most volatile policy type, likely because the absence of an excess removes the financial disincentive to file small claims.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Uncovering Loss Drivers in Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio using Data Visualisation
text:
Recommendations for Future Research

Confirmatory Data Analysis — Future studies should incorporate regression modelling to validate the findings from this exploratory analysis and establish more definitive relationships between the identified risk factors and portfolio outcomes.
Exploring Additional Variables — Variables such as driver occupation, annual mileage, claims history duration and vehicle usage type could provide a more complete picture of risk segmentation.
Longitudinal Analysis — Conducting longitudinal studies to track changes in loss ratios and claim frequencies over a longer time period can reveal trends and seasonal patterns that a three-year snapshot may not capture.
Incorporating External Data — As highlighted by the Swiss Re Institute (2019), enriching the portfolio data with external sources such as traffic density, weather patterns and regional accident statistics could further refine segmentation and improve underwriting strategy.

title: 8. Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
Reflections
Time-series visualisations go far beyond a simple line chart. A calendar heatmap uses colour intensity to reveal when events cluster, for example, showing that cyber attacks spike on certain hours or weekdays. A cycle plot is particularly useful for seasonal data because it overlays multiple years on the same month panels, making trends immediately visible. A slopegraph is elegant for comparing two time points across many categories — the slope direction and angle tell the story at a glance. The key takeaway is that choosing the right chart type for time-oriented data depends on whether you are looking for patterns within a cycle, trends over time, or relative change between points.

Plotting Calendar Heatmap
A calendar heatmap plots a grid of weekday × hour, coloured by the count of events. It reveals when attacks are most frequent at a glance.

The Data

Importing the data

There are three columns:

timestamp — date-time of the attack in POSIXct format
source_country — ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (e.g. “CN” for China)
tz — timezone of the source IP address



Data Preparation

Step 1: Deriving weekday and hour fields
A helper function make_hr_wkday() is written to take the timestamp, country, and timezone, and return a clean data table with the weekday and hour extracted correctly per timezone.

make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts,
                        tz = tz[1],
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}


ymd_hms() from lubridate parses the timestamp string into a proper date-time object, applying the correct timezone
weekdays() from base R extracts the day of the week as a character string
hour() from lubridate extracts just the hour (0–23)



Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble

wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday',
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday',
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday',
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp,
                   .$source_country,
                   .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))

Both wkday and hour are converted to factors with explicit level ordering. This ensures ggplot2 displays them in the correct sequence (Sunday at the bottom, Saturday at the top; hours 0–23 left to right).

geom_tile() draws one rectangle per hour-weekday combination, filled by attack count
theme_tufte() strips away gridlines and chart junk for a cleaner look

title: 8. Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
Plotting Cycle Plot
A cycle plot shows seasonal patterns by faceting across months, drawing each year as a separate line within each month panel. A red dashed horizontal line marks the monthly average, making it easy to see whether recent years are above or below the long-run norm.

Step 1: Data Import

air <- read_excel("arrivals_by_air.xlsx")



Step 2: Deriving month and year fields

air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`),
                    levels=1:12,
                    labels=month.abb,
                    ordered=TRUE)
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))


month() extracts the month number (1–12), then labelled with standard three-letter abbreviations (month.abb)
year() extracts the four-digit year
Both use lubridate functions



Step 3: Extracting the target country
The analysis focuses on Vietnam, filtering to 2010 onwards.

Vietnam <- air %>%
  select(`Vietnam`,
         month,
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)



Step 4: Computing year average arrivals by month

hline.data <- Vietnam %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))

This creates a small summary table with one average value per month — used to draw the red reference line.


Step 5: Plotting the cycle plot

The plotThe code chunk














ggplot() +
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year,
                y=`Vietnam`,
                group=month),
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue),
             data=hline.data,
             linetype=6,
             colour="red",
             size=0.5) +
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")




What to notice:

geom_line() draws one line per month panel, with year on the x-axis — each panel shows how that particular month has trended over the years
geom_hline() draws a dashed red line at the per-month average — lines above it indicate above-average years
facet_grid(~month) creates 12 side-by-side panels, one per month

title: 8. Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data

Plotting Slopegraph
A slopegraph compares values for multiple categories at two time points, using the slope of the connecting line to show whether each category increased, decreased, or stayed the same. It is ideal for ranking comparisons.

Step 1: Data Import

rice <- read_csv("rice.csv")



Step 2: Plotting the slopegraph

The plotThe code chunk

























What to notice:

mutate(Year = factor(Year)) converts the year from a number to a categorical label, this is required by newggslopegraph() to treat the two years as discrete endpoints rather than a continuous axis
filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) keeps only the two comparison years
newggslopegraph(Year, Yield, Country) maps time to the x-axis, the measured value (rice yield) to the y-axis, and labels each line by country
Lines sloping upward indicate yield increased; lines sloping downward indicate a decline between 1961 and 1980

Data Wrangling

Wrangling time
SentDate is imported as a character data type and needs to be converted to a proper date format. dmy() converts the date string and wday() extracts the day of the week — both from the lubridate package.

We filter to keep only work-related emails and aggregate by source, target and weekday to count the number of emails sent.

  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
  summarise(Weight = n()) %>%
  filter(source != target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

The main strength of parallel coordinates plots is that they can show many variables at once without needing separate charts. Reflections
There are several ways to visualise a correlation matrix in R, each suited for different purposes. pairs() gives a quick scatter plot overview, ggcorrmat() is useful because it layers in statistical significance automatically, and corrplot() is the most visually polished and flexible. Reordering by hierarchical clustering was a useful technique, it groups related variables together, making underlying patterns much easier to read. The significance test overlay also helped distinguish meaningful correlations from noise.

With correlation coefficients

The plotThe code chunk














panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
  if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

title: Hands-on Exercise 4d: Building Funnel Plot with R
text: A funnel plot is used for fair comparison between groups of different sizes. In this exercise I used COVID-19 data from Jakarta to compare cumulative fatality rates across sub-districts.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4d: Building Funnel Plot with R
text:
Reflections
Funnel plots were completely new to me. The key insight is that comparing raw rates between areas of different sizes is unfair, a small sub-district with 2 deaths out of 10 cases looks much worse than a large one with 200 deaths out of 5000 cases, even if the true rate is similar.
The funnel shape comes from the fact that uncertainty decreases as sample size grows, small areas sit further out in the funnel, and outliers outside the 95% or 99% limits are the ones worth investigating.
Building the ggplot2 version from scratch was challenging but helped me understand exactly how the confidence limits are calculated.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4d: Building Funnel Plot with R
text:
Funnel Plot using ggplot2

Computing derived fields

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)



Calculate 95% and 99.9% confidence limits

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq))
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq))
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq))
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq))
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95,
                   number.ll999, number.ul999,
                   number.seq, fit.mean)



Static funnel plot

The plotThe code chunk














p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label=`Sub-district`),
             alpha=0.4,
             size=0.9) +
  geom_line(data = dfCI,
            aes(x = number.seq,
                y = number.ll95),
            linewidth = 0.4,
            colour = "grey40",
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI,
            aes(x = number.seq,
                y = number.ul95),
            linewidth = 0.4,
            colour = "grey40",
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI,
            aes(x = number.seq,
                y = number.ll999),
            linewidth = 0.4,
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI,
            aes(x = number.seq,
                y = number.ul999),
            linewidth = 0.4,
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = dfCI,
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean),
             linewidth = 0.4,
             colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,0.05)) +
  ggtitle("Cumulative Fatality Rate by Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  ylab("Cumulative Fatality Rate") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size=12))
p

Reflections
This was my first time making charts interactive in R. The ggiraph package was surprisingly straightforward — just swap geom_point() for geom_point_interactive() and wrap it in girafe().
The most interesting part was the coordinated multiple views where hovering on one chart highlights the same student in another chart. This is really useful for spotting patterns across different variables at the same time.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics
text: In this exercise, I was introduced to ggplot2 and the layered grammar of graphics. I learned that every chart in R is built by adding layers — starting from data, then aesthetics, then geometry. I explored many different chart types including histograms, dot plots, box plots, violin plots, and scatter plots. I also discovered how facets allow us to split charts by categories, and how built-in themes like theme_classic() and theme_minimal() can instantly change the look of a chart. This exercise showed me that ggplot2 is both systematic and flexible.

tooltip <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = .01) {
  mean <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean maths scores:", mean, "+/-", sem)
}

text: In this exercise I learnt two relatively new statistical graphic methods for visualising distribution — ridgeline plots and raincloud plots — using ggridges and ggdist.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4a: Visualising Distribution
text:
Reflections
This exercise introduced two new ways to visualise distribution. Ridgeline plots are great for comparing distributions across many groups at once, much cleaner than stacking multiple histograms.
The raincloud plot was the most interesting, it combines three views in one chart: the density shape, the boxplot summary, and the actual data points. This gives a much more complete picture than just a boxplot alone.
The step-by-step build up of the raincloud plot (half eye → boxplot → dots → flip) was a good way to understand how each layer adds information.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4c: Visualising Uncertainty
text:
Reflections
The difference between standard error bars and confidence intervals was much clearer after seeing them plotted side by side. The 95% CI version (mean ± 1.96 × SE) is more informative than just showing SE.
The interactive version combining plotly and DT was the most practical, being able to hover over a point and see the exact confidence interval values, and then filter the table at the same time, is very useful for presentations.
stat_gradientinterval() from ggdist was visually striking — the gradient effect gives a more intuitive feel for where the uncertainty is concentrated.

A ternary plot is useful when three variables always sum to a fixed total, something a standard scatter plot cannot show. Reflections
The key takeaway from this exercise is that text data requires significant preprocessing before meaningful visualisation is possible — removing headers, signatures and stop words is just as important as the visualisation itself. Importing Multiple Text Files from Multiple Folders

Creating a folder list

news20 <- "20news/"



Defining a function to read files
A custom function read_folder() is written to read all text files from a folder into a single data frame. map() of the purrr package is used to apply the function to each file, while unnest() flattens the resulting list into a data frame.

read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder,
                    full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file,
                      read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(id = basename(file),
              text) %>%
    unnest(text)
}



Reading in all messages from the 20news folder

raw_text <- tibble(folder =
                     dir(news20,
                         full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder,
                          read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  mutate(newsgroup = basename(folder)) %>%
  select(newsgroup, id, text)

write_rds(raw_text, "20news.rds")

title: 7b. Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R
text:
Introducing tidytext

Removing headers and automated email signatures
Each message contains a header and automated email signature that are not useful for analysis. cumsum() of base R is used to return a cumulative sum, while str_detect() of stringr detects the presence of a pattern in a string.

cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()



Removing lines with nested quotes
Regular expressions are used to remove lines with nested text representing quotes from other users.

cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text,
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text,
                     "^In article <")
  )



Text data processing
unnest_tokens() of tidytext splits each message into individual words (tokens). Stop words — common words like “the” and “and” — are then removed using stop_words.

usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)

  geom_node_point(size = 6,

title: 7b. Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R
text:
Bigram Analysis

Counting bigrams
A bigram is a pair of consecutive words. unnest_tokens() with token = "ngrams" and n = 2 extracts all bigrams from the text.

bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram,
                text,
                token = "ngrams",
                n = 2)

bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)



Cleaning bigrams
Bigrams containing stop words are removed by separating each bigram into two words and filtering out those containing stop words.

bigrams_separated <- bigrams_count %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"),
           sep = " ")

bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word)



Counting bigrams again
unite() of tidyr is used to combine the two word columns back into a single bigram column.

bigrams_united <- bigrams_filtered %>%
  unite(bigram, word1, word2, sep = " ")

section: Dashboard 1 — English Score Distribution by Class
text:
Dashboard 1 — English Score Distribution by Class
This dashboard shows a boxplot of English scores by class alongside a histogram of the overall score distribution. The average English score across all students is 67.18.



English Score Distribution by Class


From the Exam Data, I noticed that 3D performed better than 3C in the English exam, as 3D has a higher overall score distribution. This shows that the boxplot is useful because it allows me to compare not only the general performance between classes, but also the spread and consistency of scores within each class.
The boxplot also helps reduce the zone of irrelevancy. In a bar chart, the viewer may focus too much on small differences between bars that may not be meaningful, making minor gaps look more important than they really are. With a boxplot, I can see whether the scores actually overlap, whether the difference between classes is meaningful, and whether the overall distribution supports the conclusion. This makes the boxplot more useful for comparing exam performance across classes.

text: In this in-class exercise, we explored Shiny, R’s framework for building interactive, web-enabled visual analytics applications. Unlike static ggplot2 visualisations, Shiny allows users to interact with data dynamically through widgets such as sliders and dropdowns — without needing to write any JavaScript or HTML.

title: In-Class Exercise 6: Designing Web-enabled Visual Analytics Application with Shiny
text:
Reflections
Building the Shiny app helped me understand the clear separation between the UI (what the user sees) and the server (the logic behind what gets displayed). What clicked for me was how reactivity works — outputs don’t just run once, they automatically re-execute whenever a relevant input changes. This is a fundamentally different mental model from writing a standard R script top to bottom.
I also noticed a practical difference between aes() and aes_string() — when the variable name comes from a reactive input (a string), aes_string() is needed so ggplot2 can interpret it correctly. Small details like this matter a lot when inputs are dynamic.

title: In-Class Exercise 6: Designing Web-enabled Visual Analytics Application with Shiny
text:
Key Concepts

Shiny Building Blocks
Every Shiny app has two components:

UI (User Interface) — defines the layout and widgets the user interacts with
Server — contains the R logic that generates outputs in response to inputs



Reactivity
Shiny’s reactivity system ensures outputs update automatically when inputs change. The key reactive functions are:







Function
Purpose




reactive()
Creates a reactive expression that caches its result


observe()
Runs code for side effects when inputs change


eventReactive()
Only reacts when a specific event occurs (e.g. button click)


isolate()
Reads a reactive value without triggering re-execution

title: In-Class Exercise 6: Designing Web-enabled Visual Analytics Application with Shiny
text:
Pupils Exam Results Dashboard

Loading Packages and Data

pacman::p_load(shiny, tidyverse)
exam <- read_csv("Exam_data.csv")



UI
The UI uses sidebarLayout() with two widgets — a selectInput() for subject selection and a sliderInput() for controlling the number of histogram bins.

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Pupils Exam Results Dashboard"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput(inputId = "variable",
                  label = "Subject:",
                  choices = c("English" = "ENGLISH",
                              "Maths"   = "MATHS",
                              "Science" = "SCIENCE"),
                  selected = "ENGLISH"),
      sliderInput(inputId = "bins",
                  label = "Number of Bins",
                  min   = 5,
                  max   = 20,
                  value = 10)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("distPlot")
    )
  )
)



Server
The server uses aes_string() to pass the reactive input$variable (a string) into ggplot2.

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$distPlot <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(exam,
           aes_string(x = input$variable)) +
      geom_histogram(bins  = input$bins,
                     color = "black",
                     fill  = "light blue")
  })
}



Running the App

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

title: Executive Summary: Motor Vehicle Insurance Loss Drivers
text:
Study Objective and Data Scope
Objective: identify visual and statistical patterns that explain poor profitability and high volatility.



Area
Summary




Dataset
Spanish motor vehicle insurance portfolio


Original data
354,140 policy records, 47 variables


Analytical data
352,338 records after missing value treatment


Period
2022 to 2024


Key outcomes
Loss ratio, claim frequency, has claim



Three derived measures drive the analysis:

Loss ratio = total incurred ÷ total premium — a ratio above 1 means the insurer paid out more than it collected
Claim frequency = total claims ÷ total exposure — higher values indicate a more volatile portfolio
Has claim = 1 if any claim was filed, 0 otherwise — separates claiming from non-claiming policies


The analysis is based on a large real-world insurance portfolio covering 2022 to 2024. After cleaning, only 1,802 records were removed, so the final sample remains highly representative. Loss ratio answers the profitability question, are we collecting enough premium to cover claims? Claim frequency answers the volatility question, how often are claims occurring? Has claim allows us to isolate the 14.3% of policies that drive all portfolio losses.

title: Executive Summary: Motor Vehicle Insurance Loss Drivers
text:
Portfolio Profile


Third-Party Combined (58%) dominates, performance issues here affect the whole portfolio
96.5% of policyholders have a Good bonus score, portfolio appears low risk on the surface
Aggregate stability can mask concentrated pockets of high-risk segments


The portfolio is heavily concentrated in Third-Party Combined policies at 58%, with Comprehensive with Excess second at 25.6%. Basic Third-Party is only 1.6% so patterns in this group must be interpreted carefully. The high proportion of Good bonus score policyholders creates a misleading picture of low overall risk, the real losses are concentrated in a small number of higher-risk segments that are not visible at the aggregate level.

title: Executive Summary: Motor Vehicle Insurance Loss Drivers
text:
Claim Occurrence and Severity


85.7% of policies record no claims but the 14.3% with claims drive all losses
Most claims cost below €2,500 — but occasional large losses have an outsized impact
The average claim cost (€1,271.98) is well above the typical claim (€898.68) a sign that severe claims are pulling the average up


Most policies do not generate claims. The 85.7% no-claim rate makes the portfolio look calm at a high level, but the smaller claiming group is responsible for all incurred costs. Most claims are relatively affordable below €2,500, but a small number of expensive claims pull the average well above the typical value. This pattern means the portfolio’s profitability is more sensitive to large individual losses than to the volume of claims.

title: Executive Summary: Motor Vehicle Insurance Loss Drivers
text:
Profitability Patterns: Loss Ratio


Most claiming policies record a loss ratio between 1.0 and 2.5, incurred costs regularly exceed premiums
The average loss ratio (2.58) is noticeably higher than the typical value (2.0), a small number of very costly policies are pulling it up
The long right tail signals that catastrophic losses, have a significant impact on overall profitability


Among policies that have made a claim, the loss ratio is concentrated between 1 and 2.5 meaning the insurer typically pays out one to two and a half times what it collected in premiums. The average is higher than the typical value because a small number of policies with extreme losses skew the result upward. These catastrophic cases are relatively rare but disproportionately affect portfolio performance.

This means that portfolio volatility is not spread evenly, it is concentrated in a minority of high-frequency claimants. Identifying and managing this group is key to stabilising the portfolio.

The portfolio remains profitable across all three years, but the direction of travel is concerning. The loss ratio barely moved between 2022 and 2023 but jumped noticeably in 2024. If this pace of deterioration continues, the portfolio could reach break-even within a few years. This trend is what motivates the deeper analysis into which segments and risk factors are driving the losses.

title: Executive Summary: Motor Vehicle Insurance Loss Drivers
text:
Key Loss Drivers: Profitability


Policy type is the strongest driver of portfolio profitability
Basic Third-Party policies are the least profitable — claims cost over 4 times the premium collected
Comprehensive with Excess is the most stable — policyholders absorb minor costs before claiming, keeping losses predictable


Policy type is the clearest differentiator of profitability. Basic Third-Party has the highest typical loss ratio, meaning claims far exceed premiums for this group. However its small size in the portfolio means the overall impact is limited. Comprehensive with Excess performs best because the excess structure discourages policyholders from filing small claims, so only more significant losses get reported. This keeps the loss ratio lower and more predictable.

title: Executive Summary: Motor Vehicle Insurance Loss Drivers
text:
Key Loss Drivers: Volatility


Bonus score is the strongest driver of portfolio volatility
Policyholders with a Bad bonus score claim nearly twice as often as those with a Good score
Past claims history is a reliable signal of future claim behaviour


Bonus score reflects a policyholder’s claims history and is the clearest indicator of future volatility. Those with a Bad score claim nearly twice as frequently as Good score policyholders. This confirms that past behaviour is a strong predictor of future behaviour in motor insurance. The portfolio appears low risk overall because 96.5% of policyholders have a Good score, but the Bad and Neutral groups contribute disproportionately to overall claim frequency.

Comprehensive with Excess — claims less often, generates strong premium and the healthiest segment


The bubble chart puts three dimensions together. How often a segment claims, how expensive those claims are, and how much premium it generates. Comprehensive without Excess is the most financially exposed as it sits in the worst position on both dimensions while contributing relatively little premium. Third-Party Combined dominates by size but its risk is driven by frequency rather than severity. Comprehensive with Excess is the most sustainable segment.

title: Executive Summary: Motor Vehicle Insurance Loss Drivers
text:
Executive Implications

The 14.3% of policies that claim are responsible for all portfolio losses, while the majority generate no cost at all. The loss ratio has risen 13.7% in three years and is steadily approaching break-even.
Policy type is the clearest driver of profitability. Third-Party products consistently pay out more than they collect.
Bonus score is the clearest driver of volatility. Policyholders with a poor claims history claim nearly twice as often as those with a good one. - Comprehensive without Excess is the most exposed segment, combining frequent and expensive claims with insufficient premium to cover them.


The overall portfolio looks calm but the underlying dynamics are moving in the wrong direction. The year-on-year deterioration in loss ratio is driven by a small number of high-risk segments, particularly Comprehensive without Excess and Third-Party based products. Bonus score is the strongest signal for future volatility. Addressing these segments through pricing, underwriting and product design should be the immediate priority.

Recommendations and Next Steps

Review pricing adequacy for Third-Party based policies
Monitor Bad and Neutral bonus score groups more closely
Investigate Comprehensive without Excess for small claim filing behaviour
Apply regression modelling to confirm and quantify exploratory findings
Enrich portfolio with traffic density, weather and regional accident data


The recommendations translate the visual findings into action. Pricing needs to be reviewed for Third-Party products given their poor loss ratios. Bad and Neutral bonus score policyholders should be monitored more closely as they claim more frequently. Comprehensive without Excess needs investigation as removing the excess removes the financial disincentive to file small claims. Future analysis should move beyond exploration into confirmatory modelling and incorporate richer external data.
